study_identification.title: Brain morphology normative modelling platform for abnormality and centile estimation: Brain MoNoCle

study_characteristics.study_objective: To develop and validate Brain MoNoCle, a user-friendly, open-source web-based platform for normative modeling of brain morphology that enables individual and group-level abnormality estimation and centile calculation. The platform is pre-trained on a large, diverse healthy control dataset and validated in clinical cohorts of bipolar disorder and temporal lobe epilepsy.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (ADHD1000; BLISS; CamCAN; Chronotype; Greene-HM; HCP; MEGUK; NCL-dementia; NIMH-IHV; NKI; OASIS3; Stanford-CR; UCLH; and other studies)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer (versions 5.2, 5.3.0, 6.0.1, 7.3.2 across different sites); standard recon-all pipeline; localGI pipeline (Schaer et al., 2012); Desikan-Killiany parcellation (68 regions); CorticalFoldingAnalysisTools for K, I, S calculation

quality_checking_detail.answer: Multi-step quality control: (1) Some public datasets included quality control as part of original study design; (2) Statistical outlier detection: GAMLSS models fitted for each structural metric and region, outliers flagged if residuals > 5 median absolute deviations; (3) Visual inspection: plots of each brain metric at hemisphere level against age for each dataset to flag outliers; (4) Cross-checking between statistical and visual detection methods; (5) Listwise deletion applied to participants flagged as outliers in any model to maintain same reference dataset across all models.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical GAMLSS with site as random effect. The mean (μ) depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and smooth function of age; standard deviation (σ) depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and smooth function of age; skew (ν) depends on sex (fixed effect) and smooth function of age; kurtosis (τ) depends on smooth function of age. Site-specific harmonization performed for new datasets by estimating site-specific mean and variance offsets relative to normative sites. For new sites with <30 HCs, site-specific mean is estimated from HCs but standard deviation uses average across normative sites; for ≥30 HCs, both mean and SD are estimated from site HCs.

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS (Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape)

response_variable.answer: Traditional metrics: Cortical thickness; Cortical volume; Pial surface area; Independent components: K (tension component); I (isometric size); S (shape/complexity of cortical folding); Also: Average thickness (T); Total pial surface area (At); Exposed surface area (Ae). All metrics log-transformed before modeling.

predictor_effects.answer: Mean (μ): Sex (fixed effect), Site (random effect), Age (smooth function); Standard deviation (σ): Sex (fixed effect), Site (random effect), Age (smooth function); Skew (ν): Sex (fixed effect), Age (smooth function); Kurtosis (τ): Age (smooth function). Data assumed to follow sinh-arcsinh (shash) distribution allowing for non-normal modeling where first four moments vary as functions of explanatory variables.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly handles multiple aspects of nuisance structure comprehensively. GAMLSS models simultaneously model mean, standard deviation, skew, and kurtosis as functions of covariates, accounting for nonlinearity (smooth terms for age), variance heterogeneity (modeling σ as function of age/sex/site), distribution shape (modeling skew and kurtosis), and hierarchical site effects (site as random effect in mean and variance). The model avoids separate harmonization steps like ComBat, which makes distributional assumptions that may not hold. Model comparison using weighted AICs tested 11 alternative models to validate the model specification.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Generalized additive models for location scale and shape (GAMLSS) using the gamlss package were used to simultaneously model the parameters (mean, standard deviation, skew, and kurtosis) of the distribution as response variables of the explanatory variables sex, age, and scanning site/batch. Specifically, in our model, the mean depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age; the standard deviation depends on sex (fixed effect), site (random effect), and a smooth function of age; the skew depends on sex (fixed effect) and a smooth function of age; and the kurtosis depends on a smooth function of age... Our model harmonises scanning site effects for mean and variance, avoiding separate steps as found in Combat (Johnson et al., 2007), which makes separate assumptions. Specifically, Combat assumes that after removing covariate effects on the mean, the data are normally distributed, and site effects on mean and variance are estimated based on this assumption. However, this is often not the case, since data may follow a non-normal distribution with higher distribution parameters of skew and kurtosis also depending on covariates.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed subsampling analysis to assess model stability. Models trained on subsets of at least 2000 subjects showed high correlation (>99.5%) with the full model in test set residuals, and mean absolute error converged around 2000 subjects, confirming model stability with the full sample (n=3276).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: We performed a subsampling analysis that showed our models stabilised, see Supplementary Materials S3 for details... Figure S3.1 A shows that models trained on sampled subsets of at least 2000 subjects have a high correlation (>99.5%) with the model trained on the full dataset in terms of test set residuals, meaning predictions from the subset-trained model closely match those from the model using all available data. Figure S3.1 B shows that the mean absolute error of predictions on the test set converges when using around 2000 subjects for training, indicating that model performance has little improvement with larger sample sizes.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The subsampling analysis in S3 used 200 randomly sampled subjects held out across sites to assess model similarity and fit, which could be considered a form of independent validation within the same domain. However, this is internal cross-validation within the training process rather than a completely independent external validation dataset from the same healthy control domain.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: 200 subject randomly sampled across sites were held out to assess model similarity and fit across samples.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study validated the normative model extensively on two different clinical domains: (1) Bipolar disorder cohort (n=56 BD, 26 HC from BLISS dataset), showing improved alignment with ENIGMA findings compared to case-control analysis; (2) Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy cohort (n=133 mTLE with 74 left and 59 right hemisphere onset, 99 HC from IDEAS dataset), demonstrating group-level replication of ENIGMA findings (correlation >0.5 with ENIGMA effect sizes) and individual-level validation through seizure lateralization prediction (accuracy 0.782 for cortical volume, 0.759 for I component). Additionally compared outputs with another normative platform (CentileBrain) showing good agreement (correlation >0.75 in ~80% of regions).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To demonstrate the utility of our normative models in predicting abnormalities in patient groups and individuals, we included two exemplar clinical datasets. A sample of 133 adults with mesial TLE (mTLE; n = 74 right hemisphere seizure onset; n = 59 left hemisphere seizure onset) and 99 healthy controls (HC-mTLE) were acquired from the recent IDEAS dataset release... We also included a sample of 56 adults with bipolar disorder (BD) and 26 healthy controls (HC-BD) from the Bipolar Lithium Imaging and Spectroscopy Study (BLISS)... Compared with the traditional case-control pipeline, in which BD patients were compared with matched healthy controls, our normative pipeline yielded abnormality estimates that were more in line with previous research, for example, a large-scale ENIGMA study... Effect sizes produced by Brain MoNoCle in our sample show agreement (correlation larger than 0.5) with those reported previously [ENIGMA]... Results show good agreement between both apps (correlation larger than 0.75 in approx. 80% of brain regions).

clinical_dataset.answer: BLISS (Bipolar Lithium Imaging and Spectroscopy Study); IDEAS (Imaging Database for Epilepsy and Surgery)

diseases_studied.answer: Bipolar disorder (BD); Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE)

clinical_groups_age.answer: BD: mean 45.36 (SD 12.15); mTLE left: mean 36.0 (SD 11.2); mTLE right: mean 38.2 (SD 10.8); HC-BD: mean 48.46 (SD 11.80); HC-mTLE: mean 39.1 (SD 12.1)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score: calculated as (individual value - predicted mean) / standard deviation, accounting for age, sex, and site effects. Centile score: calculated from z-scores using site-specific mean and standard deviation, along with skew and kurtosis from normative model. Hemisphere z-score difference used for lateralization analysis (left minus right hemisphere z-scores).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group-level analysis: Cohen's d effect sizes calculated for clinical groups vs controls, comparing regional abnormalities. BD validation compared effect sizes from normative model vs small case-control analysis, assessing alignment with ENIGMA BD findings (Hibar et al., 2018). mTLE validation: (1) Correlation of regional effect sizes with ENIGMA epilepsy study (Whelan et al., 2018); (2) Individual-level lateralization prediction based on sign of hemisphere z-score difference, assessed via confusion matrices and accuracy metrics; (3) Distribution analysis using violin plots to compare z-score differences across HC, left mTLE, and right mTLE groups. Comparison with CentileBrain platform using Pearson correlations of z-scores across regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Brain MoNoCle provides validated normative models for brain morphology analysis; the novel independent morphometric K shows superior model fit (R²=0.8) compared to traditional metrics; cortical volume and isometric size I best predict seizure lateralization in individual TLE patients (>75% accuracy).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The Brain MoNoCle platform successfully combines six key features in one web-based tool: user-friendly interface, individual and group outputs, multi-site analysis, regional and whole-brain analysis, integration with existing tools, and multiple morphology metrics. In the bipolar disorder validation (n=56), normative modeling produced results more consistent with large-scale ENIGMA findings than traditional case-control comparison (e.g., cortical thinning in left precentral gyrus d=-0.8 with normative model vs. thickening d=0.70 with case-control). In the temporal lobe epilepsy cohort (n=133 mTLE), group-level abnormalities showed good correlation with ENIGMA findings (r>0.5 for effect sizes), and widespread cortical thinning was observed especially in right mTLE (precentral gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, inferior parietal gyrus). Individual-level validation demonstrated that cortical volume and isometric size I were most effective for lateralizing seizure onset (78.2% and 75.9% correct lateralization respectively; 36.1% and 32.3% beyond 2 SD; overall accuracy 0.782 and 0.759), while traditional cortical thickness was less effective. Comparison across morphometrics revealed that the independent component K showed superior model fit to age and sex (R²=0.8 for both hemispheres) compared to all other metrics (R²≈0.4-0.6), suggesting K better captures biological variance related to these covariates while leaving disease-specific variance intact. This highlights the importance of analyzing multiple morphology measures simultaneously.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The normative dataset includes 21 sites, which is at the recommended threshold for random effects modeling; future work should prioritize increasing number of sites with diverse global representation rather than just total subject count. Current implementation uses only Desikan-Killiany parcellation (68 regions); additional atlases and vertex-wise analysis would be valuable. Platform currently does not support longitudinal data analysis, though this is planned for future development. Clinical validation focused on cortical measures; subcortical abnormalities in mTLE (e.g., hippocampal changes) were not captured. Model chose not to include site random effect on skew parameter (despite better fit in some regions in Model 6) to maintain consistency across metrics/regions and to allow application to new sites with small HC samples. Current FreeSurfer version varies across sites (5.2 to 7.3.2), though this was corrected during harmonization.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Platform available at https://cnnplab.shinyapps.io/BrainMoNoCle/ as open-source R Shiny App with three main components: (1) Pre-trained normative models for each morphological measure; (2) Back-end computing z-scores and centiles for new data; (3) Front-end user interface accepting FreeSurfer outputs directly. Users can upload csv files from FreeSurfer aparcstats2table command or CorticalFoldingAnalysisTools, along with metadata (subject ID, age, sex, group, dataset, site, session). Outputs include z-scores, group summary statistics, centiles as csv files, brain plots, scatter plots, and html reports. New sites require healthy control cohort for site harmonization (minimum >10 for mean estimation, ≥30 recommended for SD estimation). Authors plan to continuously expand normative reference dataset and add features including multiscale morphometrics, additional atlases, joint modeling of related regions, vertex-wise analysis, longitudinal modeling, subcortical volumes, and integration with CIVET and volBrain tools. The platform successfully demonstrates that investigating multiple morphology measures simultaneously is crucial both for normative modeling (different metrics capture different biological and disease variance) and clinical applications.

general_notes.general_notes: This study introduces an important methodological advance by combining multiple novel features in one accessible platform. The full list of datasets used for normative modeling is detailed in Supplementary Table S1.1 across 21 sites: ADHD1000 (n=153), BLISS (n=26), CamCAN site 1 (n=495), CamCAN site 2 (n=83), Chronotype (n=126), Greene-HM (n=22), HCP (n=678), MEGUK-Aston1 (n=29), MEGUK-Aston2 (n=69), MEGUK-Cambridge (n=71), MEGUK-Glasgow (n=24), MEGUK-Oxford (n=63), NCL-dementia site 1 (n=29), NCL-dementia site 2 (n=26), NIMH-IHV site 1 (n=48), NIMH-IHV site 2 (n=54), NKI (n=790), OASIS3 (n=355), Stanford-CR (n=40), UCLH site 1 (n=28), UCLH site 3 (n=67). Age ranges and FreeSurfer versions vary considerably across sites (age 5-95 years; FreeSurfer 5.2-7.3.2). The independent morphometric components (K, I, S) are derived from a universal scaling law of cortical folding (Mota & Herculano-Houzel, 2015; Wang et al., 2016, 2019, 2021) and are statistically independent and orthogonal to each other, accounting for covariance between traditional metrics. K (tension component) is dimensionless, relatively preserved across species, but sensitive to aging and disease; I (isometric size) captures information about isometric scaling independent of K; S (shape) captures complexity of folding as cross-product of K and I. The study includes extensive supplementary validation: model formula testing with AIC comparison across 11 alternative models (Figs S2.1-S2.3), detailed algorithm description for applying model to new data (Table S2.1, Figs S2.4-S2.5), subsampling stability analysis (Fig S3.1), ENIGMA comparison (Fig S4.1), lateralization confusion matrices (Fig S4.2), and CentileBrain comparison (Fig S5.1). Journal confirmed as 'Imaging Neuroscience' based on DOI structure and article metadata.
